I'm only part way through this book, but I think I have an idea where the author is going. It's interesting; instead of the oh-so-very-earnest stuff you read from people who are trying to 'prove' to you that out-of-body experiences exist, this author posits the possibility that there are things going on that could be known, but science has no interest in them. So he reports, and invites you to think what you like.

Now for why I think this could be a 'sleep' topic, my SO is a person with many, varied, vivid dreams, with full plots and characters. Sometimes I wonder how merely going to sleep could set free such a rich imagination; is it possible some of these experiences are real, but in dimensions we currently dismiss?

I am not good at remembering dreams, though I'm certain I often do dream. And once in a while I'll remember part of one. What I often remember is dreaming of flying, or near-flying (descending long flights of stairs effortlessly, touching down on maybe one of ten) and I've had some hair-raising takeoffs.

What do you think? Is there a 'world of sleepers' where real things happen?
Thoughts during reading a book called "Journeys Out Of The Body" by robert a. monroe

It seems silly to posit that our physical brains could have access to information that is somehow outside of our physical world. The very idea of there being information or anything else outside of the tangible world that we inhabit doesn't make a whole lot of sense to me, because the very idea of existence seems inextricably bound up in that tangible world. To be part of this world is the sole criterion for existence in my view, so things that one might posit in other "dimensions" or "worlds" are for all purposes imaginary.

I think that your SO is gifted with a superb imagination.

The very idea of there being information or anything else outside of the tangible world that we inhabit doesn't make a whole lot of sense to me,

I can quite understand on one level. But I have had some odd moments myself, nothing spectacular. One concept I have entertained is the idea that in an ordinary day, none of us have any sense of being completely interpenetrated by radio, tv, and microwaves; yet it is so, and a rich world exists on those vibrations while we go about our business undisturbed. So, I put it to you; is it possible lots is happening that we just aren't equipped to sense?

(I don't say this to bait you, nor do I have any belief one way or the other. I just enjoy thinking about it.)

Well, saying that something exists in our world and is not accessible to our limited senses is a lot more meaningful than saying that something exists outside of our world but might still be accessible to our senses. Your EM radiation example is a great one. But we've got pretty sophisticated sensing equipment these days that can observe EM, tiny elementary particles, the actual movement of light (which obviously seems to our vision to move instantaneously). We can account for most events in the world by calling upon things that are now measurable, if not strictly visible. I predict that everything that is currently outside of our artificial sensory range will some day fit under that umbrella. But yes, perhaps some things are for now outside of that artificial sensory range.

I actually listened to a podcast by neuroscientist Sam Harris recently that talks about whether psychedelic trips are a window into an otherwise inaccessible world or are instead just a novel way of interpreting our same sensory inputs. Spoiler:

I will listen. Now about psychedelics, I have had personal experience, many years ago. It's difficult for me to imagine the magnitude of the things I perceived being contained in unusual extensions of my own sensory inputs. Not to disagree, I have not yet heard the podcast.

I am enjoying this discussion, but I'm a bit at a loss about trying to make points. Something I've found valuable for my personal ethos, if you will, is to accept ideas as they come to me from others without adjudicating; that is, without applying "whether I believe it or not", or "whether I can accept this or not". I'm not talking about having 'faith', just about entertaining ideas that are not required to be 'proved' or 'framed' within what I know or believe.

Even this sounds like arguing with you, which I have no intention of doing. However, I don't see how I can speak to you about some of such things, without you 'wearing' them unproved for purposes of enlightenment. I often 'wear' a concept for a while, without debating whether it fits anything I know or think already- to see what becomes of it. Perhaps you find this obscure.

With that said, I will attest that I had personal experiences, both good and bad, and I have long lasting memories, that would have been utterly unavailable without psychedelic drugs; and I am different because of it. Do I understand? Not a thing. Did it enlighten me? Well, you'd have to be the judge. I have lost the desire to measure. Which is where I sense some fundamental difference in your approach from mine. My username reflects my appreciation of my truth, that perception of the numinous is not amenable to judgement or partition, or even understanding as we use the term. Rather, it has to mature after experience, and for me, it's not a conscious process. Sorry if that's abstruse.

I know what you mean about accepting a premise for the sake of argument, "wearing" a concept. I think of it like accepting an axiom in mathematics - it's not verifiable, but it's a basis for further reasoning. Or at least, I think that that's what you're getting at. I do try to do that, but I also have a difficult time doing that with premises that I find to have internal logical inconsistencies. I think that it's very common for people to use language in such an abstract way that it can become decoupled from logic. I catch myself doing that sometimes, even. But I try very hard not to do so, because doing so often leads a discussion down a path that can't result in getting to the bottom of the matter, finding out the objective truth or at least however close you can come to such a thing.

Anyway, sure - I'm willing to attempt to accept such a premise for the sake of argument. Let's say that during dreams one's mind reads from sensory inputs from outside of the tangible world. Do you think that different people may "travel" to the same world in their dreams; that, for instance, your dream world is the same one where your SO goes? Could you bump into one another there? :P Your dreams sound quite different from hers.

Also, consider that I sometimes experience dreams that blend (seemingly) imaginary imagery with real stimuli coming from my real bedroom. I once had a dream that I was watching some paratroopers file off of a ledge. During this dream, my real alarm clock started to play classical music. I didn't wake up right away - instead, the soldiers began to dance to the music as they ran towards the ledge. That certainly seems to me like evidence that the events in my dream were original creations of my mind, since real-world stimuli seemed to influence my creative/imaginative process.

I am hearing from you that although you far prefer irrefutable logic, you are not completely opposed to the idea of, hm, 'soft logic'; and I think that speaks very well of your mind. Not that I have some great intellectual panegyric to insert, you understand.

As to your question about people encountering one another in their dreams, I have never, and although my SO often experiences me in her dreams, I'm doubtful that it is 'me' she's experiencing. On the other hand, I feel it's likely I don't know all about myself. My unconscious self, which I don't know well but rely on quite a bit, is likely quite different from my waking person. I've no idea how that would play out in an interview on some other plane.

I have known one or two people who claim mediumship, or ESP at least; all I can really say of them is I don't know how to understand them. It feels as though they are describing the world of the sighted to a blind man. (Incidentally, both the 'mediums' I have known have taken their gifts quite as a matter of fact; there's no sepulchral atmosphere about them; in the one case, the lady I knew was often quite short with her spirit gang. They seemed to like it...)

Mr. Gilmore, I don't want to lead you on. I know almost nothing; I'm just reading this book. I like it that the author is not trying to prove anything to me, just relating experiences and in effect saying, "Make of it whatever you will". He is a bit nerdy, goes around assigning 'classes' to his experiences as though that meant anything; but I forgive, because it's pretty clear I'm not about to have such experiences; it's just a ride, another little-visited part of the midway.

My whole take on the matter so far, I'm thinking to myself, could be summed up by: " 'M'hmm?"

Well, Mr. Music, it sounds like a very interesting book. I may have a look at it.

I also doubt that she is truly experiencing the real you in her dreams. My dreams about my acquaintances tend to exaggerate my own impressions of those people, definitely in ways that are unlikely to fit with their own impressions of themselves.

Dreams and psychoactive drug trips are fascinating stuff. They show us so much about our minds. My own experiences with psychoactives have challenged my assumption that I was really aware of everything that my senses gathered.

Anyway, lovely chat. I hope that this subverse becomes popular.
